Basal metabolic rate in the Great Plains toad (Anaxyrus cognatus) was assessed through laboratory respirometry trials conducted at a constant 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Individuals acclimated to this thermal regime for two weeks prior to oxygen consumption measurements, which were collected during the inactive phase of the daily cycle. The maximum resting metabolic rate recorded was 0.0746 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0746 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that aligns with expectations for a bufonid of moderate body size occupying semi-arid environments at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This relatively modest metabolic demand reflects the species' tendency toward a sedentary, fossorial lifestyle during dry periods, when individuals remain buried in soil to avoid desiccation. The measurements were obtained from post-absorptive adults using closed-system respirometry, with chamber volumes adjusted to maintain adequate oxygen partial pressure throughout the sampling intervals. Such standardized conditions are essential for generating comparable metabolic data across amphibian taxa, particularly given the pronounced thermal sensitivity of anuran physiology. Under these controlled laboratory conditions, the oxygen consumption values exhibited minimal variation among individuals, suggesting a relatively canalized metabolic phenotype in this species. The rate of 0.0746 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 0.0746 milliliters of oxygen per hour] provides a useful benchmark for future comparative studies examining metabolic scaling relationships within the genus Anaxyrus at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C].

Egg development and hatching dynamics in Anaxyrus cognatus have been characterized under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Embryogenesis proceeds rapidly at this temperature, with the fertilised eggs completing the cleavage and gastrulation stages within a few days. Hatchlings typically emerge from the gelatinous egg mass after 4 days, with the full age at birth reached by 13 days [ab = 13 days], a relatively brief incubation period compared to montane anuran species which often require several weeks at cooler temperatures at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. The newly emerged aquatic larva, still lecithotrophic at this stage, measures approximately 2 mm in diameter based on the original egg dimensions. The wet weight at birth is 0.0042 grams [Wwb = 0.0042 grams], an exceptionally small initial mass that underscores the substantial parental investment required to reach the subsequent feeding stage. This minute body size at hatching is characteristic of bufonids that produce large clutches, as the energetic resources are distributed across numerous offspring rather than concentrated in a few large eggs. The yolk-dependent tadpoles remain non-feeding for an additional period following eclosion, relying entirely on endogenous reserves before transitioning to exogenous filter feeding. The rapid embryonic development observed at this thermal regime allows for early pond colonization, a critical advantage in ephemeral breeding habitats across the Great Plains region.

Larval development in Anaxyrus cognatus proceeds through a sequence of well-defined Gosner stages following the initiation of exogenous feeding. Under standard laboratory conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the transition from hatching to metamorphosis requires approximately 35 days , a timeframe that is intermediate among North American bufonids. Throughout this larval period, the herbivorous tadpoles graze extensively on periphyton and suspended organic matter, exhibiting pronounced aggregative behavior that may confer antipredator benefits. The onset of metamorphic climax is marked by the emergence of forelimbs, tail resorption, and skin keratinisation, culminating in the emergence of a terrestrial toadlet. This transformation represents a profound morphological reorganisation that prepares the juvenile for a fundamentally different ecological niche. The duration of the larval phase is strongly temperature-dependent, and the value of 35 days  observed at this thermal regime may be extended considerably under cooler field conditions typical of early spring breeding ponds at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. Following metamorphosis, the newly terrestrial juveniles disperse from the natal pond, initiating a period of rapid somatic growth that continues until the attainment of adult body size. The timing of this aquatic-to-terrestrial transition has significant implications for juvenile survival and eventual recruitment into the breeding population.

Sexual maturation in Great Plains toads follows a protracted trajectory, with females requiring a substantial post-metamorphic interval before reproductive activation. Under controlled conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the time since metamorphosis at puberty is 730 days [tp = 730 days], reflecting a period of approximately two years devoted to somatic growth and energy storage prior to the onset of gametogenesis. This developmental delay is consistent with a life-history strategy that prioritizes the attainment of a threshold body size before reproductive investment begins, a pattern common among anurans inhabiting unpredictable environments. During this extended juvenile period, individuals accumulate lipid reserves and mineralize skeletal structures, processes that are energetically demanding and compete with early reproduction. The onset of puberty involves complex neuroendocrine signaling cascades, including the activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which is modulated by both photoperiod and thermal cues. Once mature, females can attain an ultimate wet weight of 40 grams [Wwi = 40 grams], while males reach a comparatively smaller ultimate wet weight of 28.7 grams [Wwi = 28.7 grams], reflecting the typical sexual size dimorphism observed across the genus. This body mass difference is associated with divergent reproductive strategies, as larger females can produce more eggs per clutch, whereas male reproductive success depends more heavily on calling effort and mate acquisition rather than absolute body size.

The reproductive ecology of Anaxyrus cognatus is characterized by explosive breeding events triggered by warm spring rains, with individuals congregating in ephemeral ponds to engage in amplexus and egg deposition. Under favorable thermal conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], females deposit approximately 11,074 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 11,074 eggs per clutch] in a single reproductive event per season [F_R_i = single reproductive event per season], representing a considerable energetic investment given the modest adult body size of this species. These egg masses, consisting of long gelatinous strings, are typically wrapped around submerged vegetation to provide structural support and protection from sedimentation. The high fecundity observed in this species compensates for substantial mortality during the egg and larval stages, a demographic pattern typical of r-selected amphibian life histories. Field studies employing skeletonchronology and mark-recapture methods indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 10.7 years [am = approximately 10.7 years] when maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This longevity allows multiple breeding opportunities across an individual's lifetime, potentially buffering population dynamics against years of poor reproductive success caused by unfavorable environmental conditions. The interplay between fecundity and longevity in this species reflects an evolutionary compromise between current reproduction and survival, shaped by the unpredictable nature of prairie wetland ecosystems across its extensive geographic range.
